captions: Give the model a second input: a random index ξ from a simple noise source we control, here a standard Gaussian. One set of weights ν is shared by every index.
Fix the index ξ₁: the model is an ordinary function of x, one curve.
A different index, the same weights: another curve.
And a third.
Many indices: the curves fill the posterior band. The model pushes simple noise forward onto a distribution over functions.
A sample is one forward pass with a fresh index; an update is one step on the weights, and it moves every sample at once. The work is to train ν so that the noise lands on the posterior.
Left: functions of x with the posterior band. Right: parameter space, where the band is an ellipse around the posterior mean μ.
Take one index ξ₁. On the left it is a curve; on the right it is a single point, the parameter θ̃(ξ₁).
A second index: another curve, another point.
And a third.
Many indices: on the left they fill the band, on the right they fill the ellipse.
The model maps simple noise ξ ~ N(0, I) to a parameter μ + Aξ, which gives a function ⟨φ(x), θ̃(ξ)⟩. Its weights ν are the mean μ and M stored directions, the columns of A.
Before any data, the posterior is the prior. Draw M = 16 vectors once and keep them: the particles. Side by side they form the matrix A₀, one column per particle.
To sample, do not draw a new vector. Draw a random index ξ: one standard Gaussian weight per stored arrow.
Scale each arrow by its weight and add them head to tail. Where the path ends is the sample.
A different index, the same arrows: a different sample.
And a third. Nothing about the arrows changed; only the index did.
Many indices fill the prior. This is Ensemble++ in one picture: M stored vectors, one cheap random index per sample.
Why is this a prior sample? A linear map of a Gaussian is Gaussian, so only the covariance A₀A₀ᵀ has to match the prior.
Pick a direction v and project the stored arrows onto it.
Along v, the spread of the cloud (dashed) nearly matches the spread of the prior (solid).
It holds in every direction: a random projection that preserves lengths. M of order d is enough, by Johnson–Lindenstrauss.
Now data arrive from a linear-Gaussian model, Y = ⟨θ*, X⟩ + ω, whose exact posterior is known: the ground truth for the cloud.
The cross is the truth θ*, which the learner never sees.
The goal: at every step the covariance of the cloud matches the posterior's, for one cheap update per data point.
A data point arrives. The parameters that fit it exactly form a line (dashed); the environment noise is the gap to the truth.
Inject noise: each particle gets its own copy of the response plus a fresh draw Z, which we know. One new row in the table.
One step each: every particle moves toward its own line. The cloud now sits on the exact posterior, and the injected noise keeps its width right.
A second data point: one more row of noise, one more step per particle. Earlier rows are never redrawn, and no data point is stored.
After ten: the cloud has collapsed around the truth and its spread still matches the posterior. Memory is the M particles, nothing else.
After three data points, zoomed in: the arrows now start at the posterior mean and point to the particles. Side by side they are A_t.
Draw an index, the same simple noise as for the prior. Scale the arrows, add them head to tail from the mean: a posterior sample.
Another index, another sample.
And another. Only the arrows changed since the prior; they carry what the data taught the cloud.
Many indices fill the posterior. Given the particles, the sample is exactly Gaussian with covariance A_tA_tᵀ, so what must hold is dashed ≈ solid.
A posterior sample to act on, with no square root anywhere, if the cloud keeps the right covariance. Does it, and with how few particles?
Write the cloud as matrices: the history Φ (the prior, then one column per input), the injected-noise table Π under the prior draws, and their product.
By columns: column m of the noise table weights the whole history and gives particle m's arrow. Each particle is a random projection of the history.
By rows: a new data point adds one column and one row, and the product changes by one rank-one term. It never grows.
Tracking the posterior becomes a norm statement: A Aᵀ = Σ Φ Π Πᵀ Φᵀ Σ equals Σ when Π preserves norms on the history.
So the injected noise is a Johnson–Lindenstrauss projection of the history, maintained as a stream. How small can M be?
One particle over time. Each new particle is built from the previous one, the new data point, and a fresh draw of injected noise (thin arrows).
Now the particle picks the next input, as Thompson sampling does (thick arrows).
Follow one path: Z₁ goes into particle 1, and particle 1 picks X₂.
So the injected noise now reaches the data,
and every later input is chosen after seeing earlier rows of the noise.
With fixed data the classical lemma applies; with adaptive data it does not. With one particle the regret grows linearly, while Thompson sampling flattens.
In the linear model each particle takes one exact step: old position, plus a gain times the gap between its own noisy target and its prediction.
A network has the same shape: one SGD step on head m, with a learning rate in place of the exact gain.
Each head is a particle with a fixed random prior, trained on Y plus its own column of injected noise, from a bounded first-in-first-out buffer.
To act, one random index weights the heads: the same random combination, in one forward pass.
Nothing in the training loop changes except the targets.

A network with two inputs, the option x and a random index ξ. Each curve is the same network with a different index. Where there is data every index agrees; where there is none they fan out, as far as the exact posterior (shaded).

Three levels of one idea. In a linear model the index weights the particles; in a network linear in the index, it weights M heads; in general the index is just a second input, and where it enters is a design choice.
HyperDQN (ICLR 2022), HyperAgent (ICML 2024) and Ensemble++ (NeurIPS 2025) cover the three levels.
